title: How one outlier pulls a least-squares line
objective: Learners see that the least-squares line is the one with the smallest total squared error, and that a single outlier, whose squared error is huge, pulls that line towards itself.

recommended.why: Drawing each squared error as an actual square makes the quantity being minimised visible, so the outlier's giant square explains why the line moves.

alternative.why: Drawing the squared errors versus a standard chart: which one shows why the line moves, not just that it moves?

assumptions: 12 learners with seeded synthetic data: score = 34 + 4.3 × hours plus uniform noise of ±6 points
The outlier is one extra learner at 13 practice hours whose score is set by the slider
Ordinary least squares with an intercept; every point has equal weight
'Old line' means the line fitted to the 12 points without the outlier
checkDescription: The fitted slope and intercept equal the closed-form least-squares solution from the normal equations, and the total squared error of the fitted line is lower than for all eight small nudges of slope (±0.05) and intercept (±0.5).

learnerPrompts.predict: Before the line refits: will one low score at 13 hours change the slope a little or a lot?
learnerPrompts.explain: Look at the squares. Why does the line give up a little accuracy on the 12 typical learners to get closer to the one outlier?
